scope: The original four production source files, original module metadata/full license, and local caller-HTTP ownership glue/tests. Local changes close the Realm NAT discovery/create/renew/delete ownership chain. The public NAT interface and internal-port/protocol selection remain unchanged; the optional caller-HTTP gateway entry is a compatible source API. Upstream CI, examples and release tools are omitted.
localChanges: DiscoverNATs explicitly joins all four synchronous producers before closing the aggregate channel; uncancelable native discovery stays owned until return.
Gateway selection returns context errors after cancellation, including after native selection calls, while retaining normal preference ordering.

NAT-PMP creation validates real acknowledgments/assigned ports and retains attempted internal-port identity for cleanup; deletion sends external-port/lifetime zero and retires records only after exact matching acknowledgment and actual native completion; elapsed cancellation is retained separately as operation diagnosis.

UPnP address errors propagate; renewal failures retain their original lease; only explicit conflict responses retry onto another external port. Ambiguous creation stays charged and cannot be deleted as if its external-port ownership were confirmed.

UPnP deletion checks current internal-client/internal-port identity before destructive deletion. Confirmed absence or foreign ownership clears only the prior local obligation; query uncertainty, renewed conflict without ownership proof and real deletion failures remain debt. Parsed terminal success/714 resolves the remote obligation even after cancellation, with cancellation retained separately.
Concurrent mapper instances serialize the existing shared random-port generator; port-selection algorithm and key model are unchanged.
Controlled package tests cover completion, late cancellation, acknowledgment identity, failed/unknown effects and retry ownership without real NAT traffic.

The compatible DiscoverGatewayWithHTTPClient entry captures an explicit caller-owned client; UPnP XML and all SOAP services use it without changing global HTTP defaults. Existing non-injected entries retain their upstream client choice.

The injected UPnP discovery path uses the already-required synchronous koron SSDP provider for the same IG1/IG2 URNs and three joined discovery requests; generic gateway discovery retains its existing synchronous search. Cancellation discards late results only after all native calls have returned.

Context-aware UPnP external-address queries use the generated SOAP context API; context-free native gateway APIs remain synchronously joined. The caller retains the captured HTTP closure through terminal deletion.

UPnP records the acknowledged internal client/protocol and revokes blind deletion authority after renewal conflict 718. Uncertain initial creation cannot be adopted or destructively deleted merely because a current entry has the same target. All normal deletion also verifies current identity; the UPnP protocol does not provide atomic compare-and-delete.

Explicit defined SOAP argument/capability/authorization rejections own no new mapping; generic failure, unknown/combined errors and runtime cleanup markers remain uncertain. Generated SOAP 724/725 and terminal 714 paths are covered by source tests.

The optional caller resolver runs synchronously inside owned discovery and numeric device metadata is copied into each injected gateway. Selection, renewal and internal-address lookup never fall back to the process DNS resolver on the injected path; legacy non-injected entry choice is preserved.

Valid late NAT-PMP terminal ACKs are validated after joining and resolve the remote mapping; absent/mismatched/negative ACKs retain debt. PortMapper preserves elapsed-delete context as diagnosis rather than cleanup uncertainty.

Controlled generated-SOAP tests validate the raw case-insensitive SOAPAction header against the actual XML action and mapping parameters, then use the real generated response/fault parser, including fresh identity queries and terminal deletion.
